For full disclosure, I'm a game developer who found it was pretty straightforward to sell direct to customers, however most customers seem to prefer buying from an app store like steam or GOG. I'm a steam user myself and I appreciate/understand the convenience of having all my games in one place etc, but consider the perspective of a development team working on revshare: Everyone on the team works their asses off day and night to make the game, and on a weekly basis they get emails from new app stores offering to sell their product in return for 30% of revenue. They usually don't even have real people write these emails, they're automated template emails with <company or game name> pasted into them. If the team accepts these offers they go through an automated process filling out forms and entering bank info etc. and then they are expected to build their own page on the app store which mirrors the website they already built using their own promotional content. In the end, the app store takes a bigger revshare cut than any individual team member actually working on the product without ever having a real person (at said app store) lift a finger, their only costs are for hosting and the initial platform development.

Since app stores seem to be the future, does that mean that some day every piece of software sold will eventually have to pay a 30% platform tax to whoever owns the app store? Is that something that we, as consumers and developers, want?
As the app store becomes the universally accepted method of selling all software, does it seem fair for them to continue taking 30% of every sale?
How much do you think walmart or best buy take. Do you think all 60 dollars of the new smash goes to nintendo? 30% seems fair to me.

I agree that middle men have always taken a share of earnings, however the arrangement for brick and mortar sales is very different from an online app store. Also I believe that due to competition brick and mortar stores typically take less than 30% but of course that depends where you shop, also they aren't working on revshare but on a mark-up which is a bit different (losing money when selling below cost for example)

Would you still be willing to pay the best buy markup if you were buying from them online and having a product shipped to you? What if you had the option to buy the same product direct from the manufacturer without the markup?

I often don't like buying direct for the following reasons. When I buy from a place like amazon for example, I doing so with the knowledge that I am most likely not buying a scam. I am buying something that has gone through some kind of vetting process and I have faith in the exchange of cash for good/services. I am also comfortable know that if I have a reasonable grievance, I can get a refund within a reasonable amount of time. I am also satisfied that I am buying from a large network that has the buying power and wide reaching influence to get me a large selection and a reasonable price. I've been burned by direct buy before, sometimes never getting a product. Kickstarter is one of these ways. Not saying i'll never go direct buy, but I always prefer steam, amazon, ect.

This I agree with, and I think that the curation/vetting process is a big portion of what has made app stores popular to begin with.

My concern is that this may be the future: howtogeek.com microsoft app store scams

30% of a scam is just as profitable as 30% of a legit sale.

Edit: I admit my example was bad since MS has worked to clean it up, point is that curation and vetting is being set aside in favor of automating the app submission process. Look at greenlight for example. I do agree that the ability to report fraud is a valuable service being provided by app stores.

Why is this guy getting so much hate? Is it because you guys really hate ads so much or is there some ideological reason behind your reasoning?

For me it's practical reasons, mainly. There is an ideological component, but the main part is practical.

There are far too many exploits distributed via ads. I mean, even Yahoo ads distributed an exploit at one point!

And there are major privacy concerns with ads.

And ads cost me money.

Those are my main three concerns.

As for the ideological component, it goes as follows:

I do not wish the internet to go the way of cable. That is, I do not like the view some people have of "if I'm going to serve you information I get to take over your computer / ears / eyeballs in the process". It is a drastic step away from the concept of the web, and one that has nasty far-reaching consequences. If I'm sending your server a request, feel free to allow it, feel free to deny it. But don't say "yes but". Once you've sent the information on, don't try to impose unrealistic and arbitrary restrictions after-the-fact. Don't try to impose your views of the "correct" and "incorrect" ways to use said data.

That turned into a bit of a rant, but the gist of it is there. Computers operate at a fundamental level via copying. There is no such thing as "single copy only" without hardware "support" for said restrictions. At which point it's no longer the internet, it's your own network that has to try to stand on what little merit it has. Don't try to pretend otherwise. Intellectual property laws have a fundamental mismatch with actual hardware, and as time goes on the mismatch becomes more and more obvious.
